Lichen simplex chronicus is highly plausible given the description of 'sandpaper-like' texture and leathery thickening; though the patient denies conscious scratching, unconscious rubbing (e.g., during sleep or stress) is common and often underreported. Actinic keratosis is strongly considered due to location (sun-exposed dorsal hand), characteristic rough/scaly surface, and lack of symptoms—this is one of the most common precancerous lesions in fair-skinned adults. Psoriasis is less likely as it typically presents with well-demarcated, silvery scale, often symmetrically or at extensor sites, and frequently involves nails or other areas—but isolated plaques can occur. Seborrheic keratosis is possible but usually appears waxy, stuck-on, and more pigmented—not typically 'sandpaper-like' or minimally elevated. Verruca vulgaris is least likely: while it can be rough, it’s usually more papillomatous, often with punctate black dots (thrombosed capillaries), and tends to be tender to lateral compression—neither feature is reported. No systemic symptoms, no pruritus, and absence of nail or joint involvement further reduce likelihood of inflammatory or infectious etiologies."}
